On a song whose notes you can't edit (a capture, a starter, a published song with no copy here) the chords, sections and text notes are still yours — and a repeated section's labels copy into the repeat the same way they do on your own songs. Tap **Lasso** in the footer: **Undo**, **Redo**, **Copy** and **Paste** appear beside it (they stay while anything is copied). Drag a box from the notes up into the ruler over the bands you want (up to the chord row for chords, higher for sections and text notes — the covered bands get a gold outline), tap **Copy**, tap the ruler where the repeat starts to put the blue cursor there, tap **Paste**: the annotations land re-anchored at the cursor, a band already on the same span in the same row is replaced (never doubled), the cursor moves to their end so the next Paste chains, and one Undo takes the whole paste back. The notes are never touched — on a locked song Copy takes the annotations only, and if the clipboard also holds notes (copied from one of your own songs) Paste places the annotations and the status line says the notes stayed behind. A song saved by a newer Night Roll (read-only annotations) refuses the paste and says why. Keyboard: ⌘C / ⌘V / ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z. Ask: "copy the labels from bars 9–16 to bar 17" (edit_notes copy) does the same over bars.

## Files & Sync

**Install on the iPad**
Safari → Share → **Add to Home Screen**. Night Roll then launches from its own icon, full screen with no browser bars, works offline (the app and any song you have opened are kept on the device; instrument sounds are kept as they are first used), and its drafts, annotations and settings live in storage Safari does not evict. Updates arrive on the next launch with a network — the page is always fetched fresh when it can be. Same for Chrome/Edge on a computer (the install icon in the address bar). File → the "build" line at the bottom of the menu says "installed" when you are running the installed copy. If offline support ever misbehaves, open the site with ?sw=0 once to turn it off on that device.

**File**
Everything file-shaped lives here now. File → Settings has four tabs — **Saving** (folder or Files), **AI**, **GitHub**, **Other** (the debug log) — and reopens on the one you last used. Open… (the song picker, two sections: **LOCAL**, this device's copies grouped by folder, each row saying not published / published / changed since publish / annotations changed here; and **PUBLISHED**, the albums in your repo as folders, e.g. Imports › Mega Man 2 — a published song with a local copy opens the local one; the current song's title shows above the track chips, led by **Published** or **Local** — the same meaning as Open's two sections — then its folder: Published › Final Fantasy I › Battle Scene), **Open Recent ▸** (right under Open… — tap it to expand, in place, up to 10 songs you've had open on this device, newest first, as Title — Album; the current song shows ✓ and dimmed; tap any other to open it; **Clear recent** empties the list; an Untitled/not-yet-saved song never joins it), New song (tempo/meter → a blank 3-voice composition called Untitled N; it lives on this device until **Save Version** asks for a folder and a name — pick one of your folders or type a new one, NES/My Covers nests), Save Version (⌘S: a dated snapshot of the music AND annotations, kept on this device only — File → Versions… lists them), Publish (opens the Publish sheet: on your own songs its button commits the .mid AND the annotations together in one go — a song with no folder yet asks for a name and folder first, then publishes; on analyzed songs the same door publishes the annotations — one workflow, and what gets pushed is whatever the mode owns), Save As (a copy of ANY song, including a locked capture, into the folder you pick, annotations inherited — write a counter-line over Town), **✎ Edit** (a capture or bundled starter shows this where Edit ▾ would be — opens a small Edit a copy sheet: a name (defaulting to the title) and a folder (defaulting to My Covers, or the folder you last used — same picker Save As has), both editable; confirm forks a copy there, annotations inherited the same way Save As's does; a name clash still gets a number, "Overworld" → "Overworld 2" — the capture or starter itself is never touched), Settings… (the AI model; **GitHub** as a two-step setup — **your songs repo** and a fine-grained **token**, with **Check** confirming the pair can publish; the local folder; and under **advanced** an optional **NSF repo** for imported game files — every field saves itself when you leave it; there is no Save button), Versions… (the published copy at the top when there is one, then this device's dated versions newest first — **Go back to this** on any row: your current state is kept as a version first, so nothing is thrown away, then that version becomes what you see — for when local edits went somewhere you can't undo your way out of), Rename… (works on everything: an uncommitted draft renames its actual file; a committed/repo song keeps its filename — analysis docs and the capture pipeline reference it — and gets a display-title override written to its album.json and the manifest, so the new name shows everywhere), Import… opens the **import hub** (below) — one screen, one section per format Night Roll reads, each saying exactly what it needs with its own **Choose files…** (one shared picker underneath — a file lands in whichever section's byte-sniff it matches); a drop target in the hub takes dragged files too, Download .mid (exports any song, works in Logic), Download audio (bounces the song to a 16-bit WAV **offline** — faster than real time, silent to you, no need to keep quiet hands: the song once through, loop off regardless of an armed cycle, through the same voices/chip/sampled/game-instrument/recording paths playback uses. On the iPad app it hands the file straight to the **share sheet** — Files, Messages, AirDrop, anywhere; in a browser it downloads. A browser with no offline renderer falls back to today's real-time capture instead — m4a on Safari / webm on Chrome, still loop off, still shareable anywhere including iMessage — and says why it fell back). Compositions auto-draft to this device on every edit — find them under Open → LOCAL, in their folder, where a ✕ (tap twice) deletes the local copy from this device; Publish is what puts them in the repo, and it updates the dropdown's catalog automatically. **Drafts is not a folder — it's this device's working copies.** A song you've saved lives in its album (new songs go to Night Roll Sketches) AND keeps a drafts row here; each row says which: **never saved** (exists only on this device, no folder yet), **not published** (a local copy with no published counterpart), **published** (matches the published copy), **changed since publish** (local edits not yet published), or **annotations changed here** (only the notes differ). Imported MIDI files land there too (prefixed "local /") — they persist on this device and stay editable, but never sync to the repo; Save As forks one into a real composition. Move to… relocates a composition into any folder of yours, or a new one (files + catalog together on GitHub for a published song; a never-published song just changes folder on this device; the row names the song's current folder first); leaving Sketches adds a "moved from" note at bar 1, which is what keeps the song editable on your other devices (as "forked from" does for Save As), so leave it in place. A ＋ track chip appears in the track bar on compositions — and a **＋ drums** chip adds a GM drum kit track: its the kit gets its own labeled LANE that starts docked under your lowest melodic note — and you can DRAG it anywhere by its labels in the left gutter; the position saves as a normal synced annotation ("lane: N"), so it follows the song to every device. The working trio — hat, snare, kick — sits at the TOP of the lane, closest to your notes; below them only pieces the song actually uses appear (no toms in the song, no tom rows), and the **⋯ row** under the lane toggles the full 15-piece kit when you want to pencil something new (sticks per device). Tap a piece's gutter label to cycle **normal → solo → mute** (S in gold / ✕ dimmed; session-only, notes untouched): one tap on snare and ONLY the snare plays; solo more pieces to add them; use mute for "everything but the kick." Third tap returns to normal. Closed hats are bright (high-passed) so they cut through regular instruments instead of fighting the pulses for the same band. Delete any track from its voice & color menu (tap the selected chip again → ✕ Delete track, tap twice), penciled like any notes, played with the built-in kit, and exported on MIDI channel 10 so Logic reads them as drums. File → Open… re-reads the published list each time you open it (at most once every 20 s), so a song published from the terminal or another device appears without relaunching. A track-name playlist (.m3u) picked on its own, with no import running, names the open song's album after the fact: each line names the song with that chip slot number — local drafts are renamed in place, a published album gets its titles in one write. Settings → GitHub → **game files & instruments** is the repo your published imports' game files (and the instruments pulled from them) go to; **create mine** makes a public one named night-roll-archive under your account. **Instruments…** lists every published PlayStation and N64 game whose instruments were extracted — **Instruments in this song** leads when the open song is one of them, then every game; a game opens to **All instruments (A–Z)** or one of its own songs (labelled by the track it plays on when that's the song you have open); tap an instrument to hear it (a kit plays its first drums). Names are measured guesses. Any track in your own song can BORROW one as its voice — the voice & color menu's **Game instruments ›** family, same games/songs picker; a loaded SoundFont's presets are one tap over in the same menu, under **Soundfonts ›** (font, then a bank:program preset list) — tap one to assign it and hear it.

**Import…**
File → Import… opens the **import hub**: one screen, one section per format Night Roll reads, each saying exactly what it needs with its own **Choose files…** (one shared picker underneath — a file lands in whichever section's byte-sniff it matches, whichever section you tapped from); a drop target in the hub takes dragged files too. **MIDI** (.mid, .midi, .smf, .kar, even RIFF-wrapped .rmi — multi-select capable): ask where they belong — **Keep local** (this-device draft, annotations never sync) or **Create album** — one or many MIDIs become an album folder under drafts, audition/rename/✕ like a chip capture, and ⇪ Commit publishes them to the songs repo so annotations sync everywhere (commit rewrites the .mid as notes+tempo+meter — foreign CCs/programs are not preserved). **NES**: the .nsf, plus its .m3u if the rip has one (track names) — an NSF that needs an expansion sound chip (VRC6, VRC7, FDS, MMC5, Namco 163, Sunsoft 5B) is refused by name ("expansion sound chip <names> not supported") — the NES pipeline captures only the 2A03, and those songs keep their lead voices on the extra chip. **Game Boy**: the .gbs, plus its .m3u, same rule. A rip with **more than one chip file** (a game shipped in two ROM revisions — Zophar's Game Boy Tetris is DMG-TRA-0.gbs and DMG-TRA-1.gbs) imports all of them in one go: each playlist line names its file, the first file by name is the album's, and a song from another file keeps that file beside it in the archive. Without a playlist, every file's slots are listed on their own. **Super NES**: every .spc of the album, picked together — tagged lengths, so the loop scan is skipped. **Genesis**: .vgm/.vgz — synth voices only, no console-audio render yet. **PlayStation**: every .minipsf plus the one .psflib, picked together — reads Sony's own SEQ/VAB driver and Square's AKAO (Final Fantasy VII/VIII/IX, Chrono Cross); both play the console's own audio. **PlayStation 2**: every .minipsf2/.psf2 plus the one .psf2lib, picked together — reads Sony's stock driver (SQ/HD/BD) and Square Enix's own (BGM/WD — Final Fantasy X); both play the console's own audio. A PS2 set that's only streamed audio (Ico, XIII) is refused: "this is streamed audio, not note data — Night Roll reads sequence data (notes), not pre-rendered streams". **Nintendo 64**: every .miniusf plus the one .usflib. For NES, Game Boy, PlayStation, PlayStation 2 and Nintendo 64: a playlist (.m3u) picked on its own, later, names an open song's album (or, mid-capture, renames an already-open session's tracks). Every chip pick opens the capture panel: the same pipeline that dumped the FF1 album runs the track — loop detected and trimmed, tempo grid-fitted, the hardware loop point recorded as a loop: annotation (the capture window auto-doubles, 75 → 150 → 300s, when no loop fits) — and lands as a LOCAL draft under an album named for the game; audition and rename each one, ⇪ Commit a track or the whole album — it keeps going if you leave the menu, and it all keeps running in the background (Jobs) if you close the panel too — File → Publish import still pushes every import capture across all folders at once. **Chip audio is automatic**: whenever the app can reach a song's NSF/GBS/etc. (the live import session, this device's cache, or the public archive), NES, Game Boy, PlayStation, PlayStation 2 and Nintendo 64 songs render through the console's own sound hardware; Genesis and Super NES play through synth voices for now. **SoundFont**: one .sf2 (a fan-made game font, a better piano, anything) — not tied to a song at all: it loads straight in, a copy stays on this device (works offline, no GitHub needed) and, with a game files & instruments repo configured, pushes to the archive too so your other devices can play it; files over 50 MB ask first (GitHub itself warns past 50 MB, refuses past 100). **New song from a recording**: one .wav/.mp3/.m4a/.aif/.flac becomes a brand-new song — **Untitled N**, 4/4 at 120 bpm with three empty note tracks waiting (Edit → Pencil to write against it; ♩ Tempo from this take reads the clip's real tempo whenever you're ready) — it lives on this device until Save.

**Share a song**
Tap **File → 🔗 Share link…**: it shows the song's web link (always the public site's address, even inside the iPad app) with **Copy** and **Share…** (the system share sheet — Messages, Mail…). Only published songs have a link; a song that lives only on this device says so. The same **🔗 Share link** sits in the Publish sheet. A link is this player plus the song plus where the song lives: songs on this site need nothing more; a song published to another GitHub repo carries songs=owner/repo, so anyone who taps it hears that song from that repo, no setup — and you can open such links too (the breadcrumb then starts with 🔗 and the repo's name; everything is read-only there, your own songs are untouched, and nothing about the link is remembered). Publish also keeps a **song list in the repo's README** — every song as a player link, between two markers the app owns, the rest of the README untouched — so the repo page itself is the share page. The address bar is always a shareable link to the open song, and it is the song's path with no extension — …/night-roll/albums/compositions/nightroll/ambush. **Add .mid to the end and the same link is the MIDI file** (Logic opens it); take it off and it's the player again. Older ?song= links still open the player. The tab title and the link preview in Messages name the song first — "Threnody · Night Roll" — so a pasted link reads as the song, not the app.

**Export score**
Tap **File → Export score…**, pick **Letter** or **A4**, then **Export**: the score view's staves — the tracks it shows, your declared key and meter, nothing added — laid out as printed pages (title and album at the top, page numbers, each staff labelled with its track name, black ink; a system never splits a bar) in one self-contained HTML file named <song>-score.html. On the iPad it goes to the share sheet: **Print**, or open it in Files and use Share → Print → pinch the preview open → Share → **Save to Files** for a PDF. In a browser it downloads; open it and print (or print to PDF) from there. There is no in-app PDF writer and no print dialog of its own — the page's own print path makes the PDF. The paper size is remembered on this device. Works from any view once the song has notes; the file carries exactly what the score view would draw. No keyboard shortcut — it is a menu item.

**Data locations**
Night Roll is configured with WHERE its data lives (Sync → "Data locations ▾"): three rows — songs (.mid, album.json, catalog), analysis (.rollnotes + docs), and NSF (chip-audio source) — each with a read base URL (blank = this site; or any raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch> or local server) and an owner/repo write target. One fine-grained token, granted to every repo you write to, covers all commits; write errors name the repo they hit, and a 404 usually means the token hasn't been granted that repo. This is what lets another analyst point their own analysis repo at a shared songs corpus. Defaults: everything in this site's repo, NSFs from the public nsf-archive. In the iPad app "this site" is only the bundled starters, so reads default to the repo in Settings → GitHub (the same place Publish writes): your published songs, annotations and imports appear there once the repo is set; the starters come from the bundle either way.

**Folder on this computer**
Saving without GitHub. In File → Settings, tap **Choose folder…** and pick a folder on this computer: from then on every Save writes the song, its annotations, and its notes dump into that folder (laid out exactly like the repo — albums/…/song.mid beside its .rollnotes.json), nothing goes to GitHub, and no token is needed. The song picker lists the folder's albums alongside the site's; a song that exists in both opens from the folder. Tick **show only this folder's songs** under the folder row and the list becomes yours alone — the folder plus this device's drafts, none of the site's albums; with an empty folder the app opens straight into New song instead of Overworld. A device setting: it stays on that machine. FF1 songs still load from the site — annotate one and the annotations save to your folder. Chrome may ask for the folder again after a restart: **Reconnect folder** appears at the top of the File menu (until you tap it, reads fall back to the site). **Forget** in Settings returns saves to GitHub; the files stay where they are. Needs Chrome or Edge on a computer — Safari has no way to write files, and the row says so there. In the iPad app a .mid or chip file tapped in Files, or sent with **Share → Night Roll**, opens here as a local draft. In the iPad app there is nothing to set: every Save also writes the song into Files on this iPad (Files → On My iPad → Night Roll, same layout), where you can copy, share or back it up, and Publish still sends it to GitHub. Brave ships the door switched off: enable brave://flags/#file-system-access-api and relaunch (the row tells you). Recordings that aren't yours belong here, not in a repo (see the design docs).

**∿ Audio tracks (recordings)**
A recording — a guitar take, a vocal, a phone memo, a DAW bounce — as a track next to your MIDI voices. Tap the **＋∿** chip in the track bar (compositions and local drafts; File → Import… also recognizes audio files) and pick wav, aiff, mp3, or m4a. The clip lands at the cursor's bar as a new track named after the file, with the usual chip: M, S, color, fader, rename, ✕ Delete track. Leading silence is trimmed on arrival, so the take's FIRST SOUND sits on that bar (the status line says how much it trimmed). It plays in time with the song, loops with it (a clip longer than the notes extends the song's end), and is in the exported audio. **Slow it down and the pitch stays put**: at any speed but 100% the take is re-rendered (time-stretched, the way a slow-downer app does it) in the background — the lane says "⏳ preparing 50% (pitch kept)…" for a moment, then it plays in tune with your notes; a device toggle in the recording sheet turns that off for tape-style, slower = lower, like chip audio. Fine for guitar and voice down to about 40%; grainier below. **Tracks view** shows the waveform; **tap the clip** to select it (the status line says file, length, where its bytes are, and where it starts), **tap again to play from its start**, and in **Select** mode **hold and drag** to slide it in time (16th snap, one undo undoes; with no tool armed a drag pans, as with notes). Every other view shows a thin ∿ strip under the ruler marking where the recording plays. **Pieces:** a recording can be cut into pieces that move on their own. **Split at cursor** (the edit row's Cut, Edit ▾, or the recording sheet) cuts the selected piece where the play cursor is; **trim** by dragging a selected piece's left or right edge in Select (left trim keeps the sound where it is); **Erase** tap on a piece removes just that piece (the track stays); each piece drags separately. One undo undoes any of it. Tap the selected chip for the **recording sheet** (‹ prev / next › step between pieces): nudge **starts** by a bar, a beat, or a 16th, **offset** by 10 ms or 100 ms (how far into the file the piece starts — the last hair of alignment), **⇤ Align first sound** (re-trims leading silence to the current anchor), **♩ Tempo from this take** (reads the beat spacing of the piece — its waveform's onsets, autocorrelated over 40–240 BPM — and offers the tempo it hears plus half and double, with how strong the read is; tap one and it becomes the song's tempo at bar 1, one undo undoes; your notes keep their bar positions, so the grid moves to meet the take, which is the point; needs about four seconds of steady playing, and your own songs only — captures keep their measured tempo), **♩♩ Map the bars to this take** (the other direction: the GRID bends to the recording — it finds the beats through the whole piece, groups them into bars by the meter, and shows what it found: how many bars, the tempo range, and where the first downbeat sits; **Apply** writes one tempo change per bar from the piece's bar onward so every bar line lands on a downbeat it heard, wobble and all; **◀ downbeat / downbeat ▶** shift which beat counts as bar 1 when it guessed wrong — the correction Logic's Smart Tempo asks for too; the piece must start on a bar line, and a first downbeat that isn't at the piece's start means a pickup: shift, or trim the piece to the downbeat first; one undo removes the whole map), **Split at cursor**, **Remove piece**, **Replace file…**, and **☐ someone else's recording**: tick it for a band's track you play along with and it is never uploaded — GitHub removes such files on a rights holder's notice, and a public site is distribution. Storage: until you Save, the bytes live on this device only (the sheet says so; Safari can evict browser storage after a week away, so Save soon); Save writes them beside the song as <song>.audio/<file> — into your folder in folder mode, into the songs repo otherwise. Files over 20 MB get one question: **store as 16-bit mono WAV** (lossless for a mono source, half a stereo bounce) or import as-is. m4a/mp3 note: Safari and Chrome trim the encoder's lead-in differently, so millisecond alignment is honest only for WAV/AIFF. Not yet: recording from the mic, trimming or splitting a clip, looping a clip by itself, keeping pitch when slowing down, iPad/Safari playback of webm.

**Debug log**
File → Settings → Other → **Debug log** shows diagnostic lines in Messages, marked [debug]: audio wake-ups after you leave the app, engine rebuilds, audio state changes. Off, only real problems raise the chip. A message that repeats shows once, with ×N. Turn it on when chasing a silence, so Claude can see what the audio engine measured.

**Chip stream (experimental)**
File → Settings → Other → **Chip stream**, beside Debug log: **Off** renders a PlayStation/PlayStation 2 song's console audio whole before it plays. **On** streams it instead, a couple of seconds at a time, so a big song (FFX "Challenge") can't crash the page's memory holding the whole thing at once; any failure for a song falls back to the whole render automatically. **Auto** (the default since 2026-10-01) streams only a song that would otherwise have to downgrade quality (mono, or a lower sample rate) or refuse outright to fit this device's memory — a song that fits as-is plays the ordinary whole render either way. A device setting — the switch doesn't change what you hear, only how it gets there.

**Text size**
Night Roll's own text follows your device's text size — an iPhone/iPad's Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size → Larger Text carries straight through (Safari's Dynamic Type), no setup needed. File → Settings → Other → **Text size** (Small/Default/Large/Larger) is a second, app-level dial for a browser that doesn't carry Dynamic Type through, or to go past what it offers — it scales the TEXT only: buttons, rows and the roll/score canvas stay the size they are, so nothing you tap moves.

**Messages**
**Copy all** puts the whole log on the clipboard for pasting to Claude. Errors outlive the moment: anything warning-shaped (failed commits, unreachable NSFs, token-scope problems, even uncaught crashes) is kept in a log; the footer's Messages button shows only while something is **unread** (chrome density follow-up, 2026-10-01 pm — it used to stay lit for any non-empty log, even one you'd already read), but **View ▾ → BACKGROUND → Messages** opens the same sheet always, log empty or not, nothing unread or not. Tap to read timestamped entries, Clear to dismiss. The bottom info strip still shows the latest message; this panel is where the ones you missed went.

**Song links**
The address bar always holds a link to the open song — copy it and anyone who opens it lands directly on that song (?song=…). Local drafts are excluded (they exist only on your device).

**Save Version and Versions…**
A published song is never edited in place: you edit this device's **local copy**. When a song of yours has no copy here, **✎ Edit locally** sits where Edit ▾ would be — tap it and the local copy is made right away, no confirmation, with a footer note: editing your copy on this device — Publish sends it. Every edit is kept automatically, on this device, the moment you make it — there is no auto-save switch to turn on; nothing is ever lost to a crash. File → **Save Version** (⌘S) additionally adds a DATED snapshot of the music AND the annotations to this device's history for the song — the status line says "Version saved — only on this iPad" (or "this device" outside the app); the first Save Version of an Untitled song still asks for a folder and a name. File → **Versions…** lists them newest first, plus the **Published copy** at the top when the song has one — tap **Go back to this** on any row: your current state is kept as a version first (labelled "Before going back"), so nothing is ever thrown away, then that version becomes what you see. The gold **●** after the title means not published yet (music, annotations, or chat) — Save Version never clears it, only **Publish** does. Not connected anywhere (no GitHub token or repo, no local folder)? Neither the ● nor the footer Publish button shows — your work is still kept automatically, and File → **Publish…** still opens and explains how to connect.

**Publish**
Your edits are kept on this device by themselves; **Publish** is the deliberate step that puts a song in the repo where other devices and other people can reach it. The Publish window (the footer's **Publish** button and File → Publish… open the same door) lists every song with music or annotations pending on this device, the open song first: a line when its **music** is edited since publish, each unsynced **annotation** on its own line with a ✕ that discards that never-synced note from this device, and a line when that song's **chat** messages are unsaved (they ship with the song). The footer button's number **counts songs only** — chats never add to it. Chats live in their own **Chats** section under the songs, folded by default with its count in the fold row: tap **▸ Chats** to open it (remembered on this device) — the ✦ General chat, the ⌨ Terminal chat, and any song whose only unsaved thing is its chat, each with its own **Publish chat**, and a **Publish chats (N)** button for all of them at once. Every song's row has the same three buttons: tap **Open** to open it here, **Publish** to publish that song only (a job — Jobs shows it; one motion: done, its dialog and a floating Publish window close by themselves), **Revert** to drop EVERYTHING this device hasn't published for that song — music, annotations, AND unsaved chat messages alike — after asking (the confirm names what it drops, e.g. "Revert — drops 2 chat messages"; your current state is kept as a version first — File → Versions… brings it back; a song never published has no Revert — there is no published copy to go back to). **⇪ Publish song** ships the open song: .mid, .rollnotes.json, .notes.txt and .ask.md for your own songs; annotations + chat for analyzed ones — done, the status line says "Published ‹song› ✓" and a floating Publish window closes itself a moment later (a docked one stays). **Publish all (N)** appears when more than one song is pending and publishes every song listed — music, annotations and that song's chat; songs only, the Chats section's **Publish chats** covers the rest. The Publish window docks like the AI or Notes windows (**Dock** in its title, or drag the title to an edge) so it can sit beside the roll while you work; a publish started from a docked Publish window leaves it where it is. Needs your token once; Copy/Download the file otherwise. "Unsynced" = still only on this device. Repo ↗ opens the GitHub repository in a new tab. ⎘ Web session copies a bootstrap instruction — paste it into a fresh Claude Web chat and it clones the repo, reads WEB-SESSION.md from disk, and has everything it needs to run an analysis session (process rules, file locations, session shape, handoff format). It copies the clone command rather than a URL on purpose: a session that starts by fetching keeps fetching, one file at a time, and can't grep across your notes.

## AI

**AI**
Talk to an AI tutor about what you're looking at. Tap **AI** in the top bar. Every message you send carries the song, your cursor, the lasso, your own annotations, and the notes of the bars in view (or the ruler-selected range), so "what's happening in bar 9?" means YOUR bar 9 — bars and beats are the ones on your ruler, in your declared meter. Say the word and it will also **add, edit, delete, or publish** an annotation — never on its own; ask it to change or take back the wrong one and it edits or deletes that exact annotation in place (never a duplicate left beside it), and asking it to publish runs the same Publish the footer button does. Ask can also **write notes on your own songs** when you ask it to — spell it out ("a C3 gallop on the triangle in bar 5" means an eighth note plus two sixteenths, not the word "gallop") and it lands at once as one undo step; it never volunteers a note you didn't dictate. Ask can **repeat bars**: "repeat bars 5–6 after bar 6" copies them and moves the rest later, on every track, as one undo step. Ask can also **run the Drummer** on your own song — the same generator as the Drummer button, never hand-written hits: say the bars or one of your section labels and what you want ("redo the intro following pulse1 and pulse2 instead of the triangle", "the A part again with a bit less energy", "bars 9–16, fills off, half feel"). It replaces only that range's drum hits, as one undo step; the reply names the seed, so "that one again, quieter" replays the same take with one knob changed, and the take shows up in the Drummer sheet's take chips. Energy sets busy and hard together; busy, hard, fills, feel, parts and follow (which tracks the kick listens to — any tracks by name, chords, or off) can each be named on their own. And it can **act** in the app: "go to bar 13 and play", "stop", "loop bars 5 to 12", "undo that" — several in one breath run in order, and a quick one answers with a single line and no further reply. The full list, with a phrase for each, is **AI commands** below.

**✦ Annotate this song…**
**Normal mode only** — in Learning mode the item does not exist: the analysis is yours to make. Tap **View ▾ → Mode → ✦ Annotate this song…** (no keyboard shortcut) to ask the AI model from Settings for **estimates** of this song's sections, chords and key, read from the notes plus computed facts (which bars repeat, how the bass moves, ranges, rhythm). Tick **Sections**, **Chords** or **Key** to choose what it may write, then **Run** — nothing is written before that tap, and never on its own. Every annotation it writes is tagged **✦ AI** in All notes, so you always know which lines are the model's; your own annotations are never overwritten — an estimate that overlaps one of yours is skipped, and the status line says how many. A run is **one undo**; **Clear AI annotations** removes every tagged one at once (also one undo). A long song goes to the model in bar windows and the answers merge; a reply the app cannot read writes nothing. They are estimates: check them by ear before you keep them. Unsynced until you Publish, like any annotation. Switch back to Learning mode and every **✦ AI** annotation is **hidden, never deleted** — gone from the roll, All notes, the LCD key and the ✦ Ask context until you switch to Normal again.

**House rules**
**🎓 Learning mode** (Settings → Other): hints and direction first — it confirms or refines a guess you've made, and tells you outright only when you insist or say you give up; general theory questions it answers directly; it never reveals a key you haven't set. **Normal mode**: it answers music questions directly — keys, chords, cadences, form — and says how sure it is; an estimated key is named as an estimate, not a fact. Either mode, it never annotates on its own initiative or answers a question you didn't ask.

**Move a sheet**
Where you leave a sheet is where it reopens on this device, size included (the first open is centered). Drag any sheet by its title line (AI, SETTINGS, the capture panel's title row…) to slide it aside — say, to keep the capture panel in view while you talk to the AI; drag the **◢** in its bottom-right corner to resize it. Both come back to the defaults the next time it opens.

**Dock right (and left, and bottom)**
Your window layout comes back after a relaunch: whichever of these windows were open reopen exactly as you left them — docked on their side at their width, or floating where you put them. Tap **Dock** beside AI, ALL NOTES, INSTRUMENTS, JOBS, MIXER, or PUBLISH (the Publish window) to open its menu: **Left**, **Right**, or **Bottom** pin it to that edge instead of a floating window — no backdrop, so you can keep working the roll (tap, edit, play) with it open, the song laid out in what's left. Once docked to a side, the same menu offers **Full height** (edge to edge, beside the header and footer too) or **Beside the roll** (the header rows above and the footer below stay full width — only the roll narrows). Drag the strip on the dock's inner edge to resize it — 280px up to nearly the whole window, leaving only a thin strip of the song's edge showing, so you can shove the roll out of the way for a minute and drag back (double-tap the strip to reset it to the default width). Dropping a window's title on a side that already holds one makes a **tab group** there — a small strip of tabs above it, one shown at a time; tap a tab to switch, and closing a tab's window just drops its chip from the strip (it's still docked — reopen it and the chip comes back). The bottom dock can hold two windows side by side — dock a second one there and a divider splits them; drag it to change the split, and drag the strip along the bottom dock's top edge to resize its height (160px up to nearly the whole window, same double-tap-to-reset). **Float** undocks a window again, right where it was — or just drag a docked window's title back out into the middle. **Drag-to-dock:** instead of the menu, grab a window's title and drag it to an edge — a highlight shows where it'll land (the outer part of a side edge for full height, the inner part for beside the roll); let go to dock there, or in the middle to float. Remembered on this device — reopening a window re-docks it if you left it docked; closing one frees its space without undocking it. On a phone-width window the **Dock** button is hidden and every window is always floating — there's no room to give the song.

**Jobs**
The footer's own **Jobs** button (chrome density follow-up, 2026-10-01 pm: back on the bar's right end, moved out of the now-gone More) shows only while something's running or unresolved; **View ▾ → BACKGROUND → Jobs** opens the same list always, even with no jobs at all, so a finished one stays reviewable after the footer button's gone quiet. Captures and publishes run as background jobs: start one and close its panel — tap **Jobs** for the list (title, a progress bar, progress text like "12/92 · Frog's Theme 40%", and per job **Open** to get back to its panel, **✕** to cancel a running one or dismiss a finished one, and to retry what is left). Done and cancelled jobs clear themselves a few seconds after they end, and the footer's Jobs button itself hides once none are left; a **failed** or **interrupted** job stays until you retry or ✕ it — those are the ones to look at. A job never cancels because you closed its panel; it pauses while the app is in the background and picks up where it was. If the page dies mid-run, the next open marks the job interrupted with its last counts: a retry re-runs the tracks not yet saved when the same files are still open, and says to Import them again otherwise (saved tracks are kept and skipped). One capture at a time; one publish per folder; one Publish all at a time.

**Publish dialog**
Starting a folder's publish from Open → LOCAL, or tapping **Publish all** in the Publish sheet, opens a dialog for that one job: an overall bar, a row per song (its title, and a state — **…** queued, a small bar while it runs, **✓** done, **⚠** failed with the error), the job's own note line, **Cancel** while it's running (stopping it between songs — what's already published stays published), **Retry** once it has failed or was interrupted (what is left of that same job — the same songs, not everything pending), and **Close** always. Closing it never cancels the job — reopen it from Jobs' **Open** on that job any time. Started from one song's own **Publish** row it is one motion: the Publish window stays under it while the song publishes, and when that is done the dialog closes itself and takes a floating Publish window with it (a docked one stays — its list just loses the song), leaving "Published ‹song› ✓" on the status line; if it fails, both stay — the error in the dialog and **Retry** beside Close. Publish all and Publish chats keep the dialog up, with its several outcomes to read. It is a passing window, so it floats and has **no Dock** button (drag it by its title if it is in the way); the Publish window itself is the one that docks. Capture jobs still open the familiar capture panel.

**⧉ copy / links**
Every bubble ends with a small **⧉**: tap it to copy that message whole, ready to paste anywhere (it says ✓ copied for a moment). Web addresses in a bubble are tappable and open in Safari, in a new tab, so a link the AI gives you is one tap away.

**Speak / ■ Stop listening / ■ Stop reply**
Tap **Speak** to dictate a question; while it listens the same button reads **■ Stop listening** (your words still land in the box). The other stop, **■ Stop reply** beside Clear chat, cuts a slow reply short and re-enables Send — Send stays disabled while a reply is cooking.

**Paste**
Tap **Paste** beside Speak to drop whatever is on the clipboard into the message box **without opening the keyboard** — dictate with Superwhisper (or copy anything), then one tap. The text lands at the end of what is in the box (at the cursor if the box is already active), with a space where it needs one; it is kept as your unsent draft and is never sent on its own. The first time, iOS asks with its own small Paste bubble — allow it. If Speak is listening, Paste stops it first and what is already in the box stays. An empty clipboard or a refused permission is one line on the status line, nothing else. Keyboard: **⌘V** in the box does the usual.

**Slow replies**
Your question is saved the moment you send it, so you can close the sheet or leave the app while a slow reply cooks: on the Claude Code bridge the answer keeps coming and lands when you come back (on other servers a dropped connection is reported so you can ask again). Close the sheet and keep working on the song: when the reply lands, a gold **reply** badge appears in the footer, where Messages reports errors, and the info strip says so — tap the badge (or AI) to read it. The reply goes to the song you asked from, even if you have moved to another one.

**General chat**
At the top of AI, **♪ this song** / **Ask** / **Terminal** (only with the Claude Code bridge) pick which chat you are in. The general chat is not about any one song — the app, the project, music in general, messages for the terminal — so it carries no song context, cannot add annotations, and keeps its own memory on the bridge. Its log is a repo-level file (ask/general.ask.md) that the PUBLISH sheet's Chats section ships with a **Publish chat** button (Publish all is songs only; **Publish chats** covers it). The choice is remembered on this device.

**New since your last message**
On the Claude Code bridge, every message you send — ♩ this song, Ask, or Terminal — carries what’s changed since your last one in THAT chat: any new error messages, any new status-line readouts (footer/Status window), and on Ask/Terminal (which have no song context of their own) which song is open, its view, and your cursor. You never copy an error or a status line over by hand, and a line already sent is never repeated.

**Notes from the Mac**
On the Claude Code bridge each song's chat is one long-running session that remembers earlier turns, and it can carry a message to the Claude Code sessions in your terminal ("tell the terminal to push the Game Boy branch"). When the terminal writes back, the note appears in AI as a gold **✉** bubble (inbox), and the **AI** button shows ✉ until you open it. Notes are saved with the chat.

**What Claude Code is doing now**
On the Claude Code bridge, **AI**'s own aria-label names whether the terminal's Claude Code is working or idle — refreshed every 10 seconds — with no visual badge on the button itself any more (chrome density follow-up, 2026-10-01 pm, Josh: the small pulsing dot that used to mark it was "always there and distracting"). Open AI for the full line — **Claude Code working: …** or **Claude Code idle** — in a fixed two-line strip that never grows or shrinks as the status changes (so it can't nudge the chat log above it); tap that line for the last ten steps with their times and the latest commits. Without the bridge (LM Studio, no AI) none of it appears.

**Update countdown**
On the Claude Code bridge, when a new version is about to be installed on your iPad, **AI** turns gold and counts down (**AI · 15**) and the status line says the app will restart — finish your gesture; your edits are kept as you go. It shows **AI · ⟳** while the install runs. Tap **AI** during the countdown for a small sheet — **Install now** or **Not now**. **Not now** holds the install (the Mac waits — nothing relaunches under you): the button reads **AI · ⏸** and the status line says the update is waiting; tap **AI** again whenever you're ready and choose Install now. Before the FIRST warning, if your edits aren't already in a Version, one is saved automatically, labelled "Before update HH:MM" (see Save Version and Versions… below) — one more way back if anything goes wrong. A gold banner at the top of the screen counts down too, with **Not now** and **Install now** right on it.

**Backups on your Mac**
On the Claude Code bridge, every edit to one of your own songs (a composition or a local draft) is also copied to the Mac a few seconds after you stop typing — off this device entirely, same content Publish would push. It's a safety net, not something you manage: nothing in the app reads or restores from it, and a Mac that can't be reached just means the copy waits for next time (it never blocks or interrupts an edit).

**Screenshot to Claude**
On the Claude Code bridge, tap **＋** beside Speak, then **Screenshot of Night Roll** to send Claude a picture of the app: the AI panel steps aside (unless it's docked), the picture goes to your Mac, and a thumbnail chip appears above the box — add what to look at and Send. Do it again (up to 4 per message) to attach several at once; each gets its own thumbnail and its own ✕, or tap the chip row's ✕ to drop them all. In a browser, pick this tab when it asks what to share. The same ＋ menu's **Photo Library…** attaches a picture **from Photos** (or takes one, or picks a file) instead of the app itself — the same 4-per-message limit, thumbnails, and Send line; a huge picture is downscaled and an iPhone/iPad HEIC photo is converted automatically, so it always reaches Claude as a plain JPEG or PNG.

**Terminal tab**
Two pickers at its top choose the model the terminal gives its **advisors** (read-only reviews) and its **builders** (the agents that write code) — Opus, Sonnet, Haiku or Fable; the terminal session's own model is set at the Mac (/model). The Terminal tab in AI sends your message **straight to Claude Code in the Mac's terminal** — the session that builds Night Roll — instead of the Ask tutor. Its answers come back in that tab, and the **Now:** line shows what it's doing; if it's busy, your message waits in its queue. Screenshot works the same. If the Mac can't be reached, the message goes back into the box. Its log is the repo-level ask/terminal.ask.md, shipped from the PUBLISH sheet's Chats section with its own **Publish chat** button (Publish all is songs only; **Publish chats** covers it) — it is a chat, never a song.

**The chat is part of the song**
The conversation is kept per song, whole, and it is part of the song's save: File → Publish appends everything since the last publish to <song>.ask.md beside the song (your session log — hand it to a code session later), the ● after the song title lights while chat is unsaved, and the Publish sheet lists it. **Clear chat** starts a fresh session on this device (it asks first if anything is unsaved; the .ask.md keeps what was saved) — on the Claude Code bridge it also tells the Mac to really start over: without this, the same long-running Claude session kept being resumed underneath a cleared-looking chat.

**Session usage and Compact**
On the Claude Code bridge, a small line under AI's tab strip says **"N turns · ~Nk tokens · $N.NN"** for the chat you're in (♪ this song or Ask — not Terminal, which has no session of its own), refreshed after every reply and whenever you switch tabs; past 40 turns it adds **"— long, Compact saves tokens"**. Tap **Compact** beside Clear chat (in-app confirm) to have the bridge summarize this chat's memory on the Mac and shrink it — the status line then reads **"compacted: 172 → 1 turns · ~24k → ~3k tokens"**, the exact before/after the Mac measured. Compact only affects the Mac's memory of the conversation, never your saved messages or the .ask.md log. The **plan usage** line in AI's Recent (tap the **Now:** strip) shows this account's own subscription usage — this session and this week — when the bridge has seen it.

**AI setup, step by step**
Everything below runs on a Mac (or any computer) you own; the iPad then reaches it over your private Tailscale network. **LM Studio**: load a model, then start its server with CORS on — Developer tab → Start Server, and in Server settings turn on **Enable CORS** (or in Terminal: lms server start --cors; this does not survive a reboot unless LM Studio itself starts at login). Its address is http://localhost:1234. **Ollama**: it must allow the app's origin — quit Ollama, run launchctl setenv OLLAMA_ORIGINS "*", start Ollama again. Its address is http://localhost:11434. **From an iPad** (it can only talk to https): install Tailscale on the Mac and the iPad, signed in to the same account; in the Tailscale admin console → DNS turn on MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates; then on the Mac tailscale serve --bg 1234 (approve Serve once from the link it prints). The iPad's address is then https://<mac-name>.<tailnet>.ts.net. Undo with tailscale serve --https=443 off. **The Claude Code bridge** (needed for Claude Code, the Terminal tab, screenshots and Backups on your Mac): in the Night Roll folder run npm run bridge — or keep it running across reboots with sh tools/launchd/install.sh --claude full --upstream lmstudio=http://localhost:1234 (--uninstall removes it). It listens on port 8787; expose it to the iPad with tailscale serve --bg --set-path /claude 8787 and set the iPad's Settings → AI address to https://<mac-name>.<tailnet>.ts.net/claude. It also lists LM Studio and Ollama models when they're running. Add --token <secret> to lock it and put the same secret in Settings → AI → API key. Then Settings → AI → **Test**: it lists the models it can reach, or says exactly what's wrong (server off, CORS off, http from an https page, no answer).

**Where the model runs**
File → Settings… → **AI model**. **In this browser**: pick a small model (0.4–4 GB), the first Ask downloads it once and it runs on this device's GPU, nothing leaves the device; Test checks WebGPU and whether it's downloaded. **On a server**: the URL of an OpenAI-compatible server — LM Studio or Ollama on this computer (http://localhost:1234) or on another machine on your network — plus an optional API key; **Test** lists the server's models, picks one (your last pick if the server still has it), saves, and names exactly what's wrong when it can't (server off, CORS not enabled, https page talking to an http server, no answer in 8 s). On an iPad the server must be https (Tailscale Serve). The first time you point it at a machine other than this one, it asks once before sending your notes there.

**Settings save themselves**
Every Settings field saves itself the moment you leave it — there is no Save button and closing never loses anything.

**Asking it to act**
"put an F#m chord annotation on 21.1", "mark bars 6–12 as section A", "set a tempo of 192 at bar 6" — it writes exactly that annotation (unsynced, with a ✕ in the Publish sheet like your own). "compare this to ambush" makes it read that song's notes and annotations from the repo. "Open Graveyard" (or "Open Graveyard and play it from bar 9") opens that song the way Open Recent does — once the reply has landed, never mid-answer — and moves you to Graveyard's own chat, with a gold ↪ line quoting what you asked from the song you left; the rest of your request is sent again there, in your words, so Graveyard's AI does it with Graveyard's notes in front of it (if that chat holds an unsent draft of yours, it waits as a one-tap chip instead of sending). Songs on this device count too; two songs with the same name make it ask which. Say it the way you'd say it to a person; if a name is ambiguous it asks which one, never guesses. Every command it knows is listed next, each with a phrase that works.

**AI commands**
Everything you can tell Ask, one row each — a phrase that works, then how to phrase your own. Several at once run in order ("go to bar 13 and play"); a quick one (go to, play, stop, select) answers with its one line and nothing more. Ask only ever does what you asked in that message. Generated from the app's own action list, so this is exactly what it can do today.

**Ask: write one annotation in the user's words**
**“Put an F#m chord on bar 21.”** Say the kind (chord, section, key, tempo, loop, meter, chop, note), the text in your words, the bar and beat. (act: add_annotation kind text bar beat end_bar? end_beat? comment?)

**Ask: add a track (one undo removes it)**
**“Add a track called pad.”** Say the name, and a voice if you want one picked now (else it starts auto). (act: add_track name voice?)

**Ask: play|next|prev|leave an album run**
**“Play the FF1 album.”** Name the op: play (name the album, and a song in it to start from), next, prev, or leave. (act: album op album? song?)

**Ask: run the Bassist over bars or a section label (one undo)**
**“Bass line for bars 1 to 16, busy 2, follow the drums.”** Say the bars or one of your section labels, then what you want: style (chug, pump, arp, walk, riff), busy 1–5, octave 1–3, what it follows (drums, chords, or a track name); name a track to pick where the bass goes, else it uses your bass track or makes one. "that one again, quieter" works because the reply names the seed. (act: bassist from_bar to_bar|section track? style? busy? octave? follow? seed?)

**Ask: repeat bars: open a gap, copy the music into it (one undo)**
**“Repeat bars 5 and 6 right after themselves.”** Say the bars to copy and where the copy lands. (act: copy_bars from_bar to_bar at_bar)

**Ask: remove one existing annotation**
**“Delete the note at bar 16.”** Say which one — bar and beat, plus its text if two share the spot. (act: delete_annotation id|bar beat match_text?)

**Ask: delete bars; everything later slides left (one undo)**
**“Delete bars 30 to 32.”** Say the first bar and how many (or the last bar). (act: delete_bars from_bar count)

**Ask: delete a track (one undo brings it back)**
**“Delete the empty track.”** Say which track. (act: delete_track track)

**Ask: run the Drummer over bars or a section label (one undo)**
**“Drums for bars 5 to 12, a bit less energy, following pulse1 and pulse2.”** Say the bars or one of your section labels, then what you want: energy 1–5 (or busy/hard apart), fills, feel, which parts, what the kick follows; "that one again, quieter" works because the reply names the seed. (act: drummer from_bar to_bar|section energy? busy? hard? fills? feel? parts? follow? seed?)

**Ask: change an existing annotation's text or place**
**“Change the chord at 14.1 to G7.”** Say which one (its bar and beat, or its text) and the new text or place. (act: edit_annotation id|bar beat match_text? text comment? new_bar? new_beat? new_end_bar? new_end_beat?)

**Ask: bulk-edit existing notes over bars + tracks (one undo): delete quantize velocity split join divide dedupe transpose move copy to_track shape**
**“Delete the notes on pulse 1 in bars 5 and 6.”** Say the op, the bars (or a section label) and the track(s) by name. Delete, quantize (grid "1/16", strength — default a hard snap), velocity (vel: 80, or +10/-10), split (at_bar/at_beat, else in half), join, divide (into: N), dedupe; "move bars 9 to 12 on pulse 2 up an octave" (transpose: semitones and/or octaves, or scale_steps in your declared key — no key declared, no in-key move); "move it two beats later" (move: bars/beats, negative = earlier); "copy the pulse 1 line in bar 3 to pulse 2, an octave down" (copy: at_bar, at_beat, to_track, semitones/octaves; labels: true brings the chord, section and text annotations over those bars along, chord labels shifted with the notes, as Paste to… does); to_track (move them onto another track); shape (the loudness inside each held note, no new attack: shape swell, fade, swell_fade or flat — flat clears it — or points [[beats after the note starts, level 0–127]…]). (act: edit_notes op from_bar to_bar|section tracks + op's own)

**Ask: move the cursor there, scrolled into view**
**“Go to bar 13.”** Say the bar, and a beat if you mean one ("bar 13 beat 3"). (act: go_to bar beat?)

**Ask: the action list, or one action's full text**
**“What can you do?”** That lists them; "help with drummer" gives one action's details. (act: help name?)

**Ask: insert empty bars; everything later slides right (one undo)**
**“Insert two empty bars at bar 9.”** Say where, and how many. (act: insert_bars at_bar count)

**Ask: write the last ~60s you noodled on the keys, at the cursor (one undo)**
**“Keep that on pulse 1.”** Say which track if it isn't the one already selected. (act: keep_that track?)

**Ask: the songs here: albums, titles, paths**
**“What songs are there?”** It lists albums, titles and paths — the ones on this device too. (act: list_songs)

**Ask: open another song — the chat moves there; put it LAST**
**“Open Graveyard and play it from bar 9.”** Name the song (its title, file name or path); whatever you asked for after that is sent again in that song's chat, in your words. If two songs share the name it asks which. (act: open_song song then?)

**Ask: play from the cursor, or from a bar**
**“Play from bar 17.”** "Play" alone plays from the cursor; name a bar (and beat) to start there. (act: play from_bar? beat?)

**Ask: publish the open song (the footer's Publish)**
**“Publish.”** Just that; it runs the footer's Publish and reports what happened. (act: publish_song)

**Ask: read more bars of THIS song, live state**
**“What's on the triangle in bars 40 to 48?”** Say the bars, and tracks if you want fewer. (act: read_bars from_bar to_bar? tracks?)

**Ask: read another song's annotations**
**“What did I write in Graveyard's notes?”** Name the song. (act: read_notes path)

**Ask: read another song's notes (optional bar range)**
**“Compare this to Ambush.”** Name the other song; add bars ("bars 1 to 8 of Ambush") to keep it short. (act: read_song path from_bar? to_bar?)

**Ask: ruler selection; ▶ loops it unless cycle: false**
**“Loop bars 5 to 12.”** Say the first and last bar; "select" instead of "loop", or "no cycle", marks them without looping; "clear the selection" drops it. (act: select from_bar to_bar? cycle? clear?)

**Ask: a device preference: album_order, octave_numbers, debug_log, chip_stream, sound, beat_subdivisions, volume_slider, or text_size**
**“Turn the debug log on.”** Say the name and the value: album_order (game or az), octave_numbers (on/off), debug_log (on/off), chip_stream (on/off/auto), sound (chip or midi — what you hear), beat_subdivisions (true/false — the counter's e/&/a and +NN%), ruler_highlight (true/false — whether tapping a chord/section band selects its bars), volume_slider (true/false — the top bar's 🔊 master volume), or text_size (small/default/large/larger). (act: set_pref name value)

**Ask: mute, solo, hide, volume, pan, voice or patch, color, rename or octave-shift a track (one undo)**
**“Mute the noise channel.”** Say the track and what to change: mute/solo/hide (true/false), volume (0–1.5), pan (-1 left to 1 right), voice (a name from the voice menu — unknown names list the choices), patch (a preset like Chip lead, or changes like attack=0.02 vib_depth=0.4), color (a hex code), name (rename it), or octave (1 or -1). (act: set_track track mute? solo? hide? volume? pan? voice? patch? color? name? octave?)

**Ask: new, save_version, versions, save_as, rename, or share_link**
**“Save a version called before drums.”** Say the op: new (a title, and a folder if you want one besides the default), save_version (a label, else "Version N"), versions (lists them), save_as (a title, and a folder), rename (the new name), or share_link. (act: song_file op title? folder? label?)

**Ask: add|edit|delete a titled song note (general or open question)**
**“Add a song note called Sway: long-short-long is the strongest, see bars 5 and 12.”** Say add, edit or delete, the note's title, and its words; "rename Sway to Lilt" changes the title; "as an open question" (or "mark Sway as an open question") makes it one. (act: song_note op title new_title? text? kind?)

**Ask: stop playback**
**“Stop.”** Just that. (act: stop)

**Ask: undo the last edit(s); redo: true redoes**
**“Undo that.”** "Undo the last three" for several; "redo" to redo. (act: undo steps? redo?)

**Ask: write dictated notes on a named track (one undo)**
**“On pulse 2, write C5 at bar 3 beat 1, an eighth, then D5 on beat 1.5.”** Say the track, then every note: pitch, bar, beat, length (a "gallop" must be spelled out as its three notes). (act: write_notes track notes[{pitch bar beat dur_beats vel?}] replace{from_bar from_beat? to_bar? to_beat?}?)

## Analysis

### THE ONE-SCREEN LIST

**Not a form — a checklist**
A full analysis covers sixteen things in five groups, in the order a working analyst takes them: form first, because every other item is asked phrase by phrase, and form is what tells you where the phrases are. Read the list once, mentally tick it off against your own annotations, then open any section below for the full explanation of one line. Nothing here names a key, a chord, or a reading of any real song — it's reference text, the same for every song you open.

**Form**
**1** Sections — where the music starts over or changes idea. **2** Phrase lengths — how many bars each one takes. **3** Phrase pairing — do phrases come in question-and-answer pairs, or repeat with a changed ending?

**Harmony**
**4** Key and chords. **5** Roman numerals — what job each chord does in the key. **6** Cadences — where a phrase comes to rest, and how. **7** The bass line, read as its own melody. **8** Where the harmony pulls (tension) and where it settles (release).

**Melody**
**9** Which scale degree the tune lands on at phrase ends. **10** The melody's shape — steps or leaps, rising or falling, where the high point sits. **11** Motifs — short ideas that return changed.

**Texture & rhythm**
**12** Which voice carries the tune, which the harmony, which the bass — and where they swap. **13** The rhythm and the groove — any ostinato, how often the chords change, where the pattern breaks. **14** What the music is doing in the scene it plays under.

**Summary**
**15** What the piece does and why it works, in your own words. **16** How it compares with the same composer's other pieces.

### FORM

**Sections, phrases, and pairing**
**What to find:** A **phrase** is the smallest complete musical sentence — long enough to make a point, short enough to breathe in one go; most game loops build theirs in 4 or 8 bars, so a 3- or 5-bar phrase is worth a note the moment you spot it. A **section** is one or more phrases that share an idea (the same material, or the same job — intro, loop body, turnaround); it ends where the idea changes or the music starts over. Phrases often come in pairs: an **antecedent** (the "question" phrase, ending open) answered by a **consequent** (the "answer" phrase, ending closed) — together the two make a **period**. A **sentence** is the other common pairing: a short idea stated, immediately repeated, then pushed on into a new, often faster-moving continuation. A period often starts both phrases the same way and changes only the ending — open the first time, closed the second (a **parallel period**). **How to find it in Night Roll:** Drag along the bar ruler to hear a candidate phrase on its own — a drag arms the cycle and loops just that span, so you can audition "does this sound like one idea?" without re-selecting. Once you're sure, select the range and **+ Note → section**, with a short label (A, B, A′…); sections nest by containment, so an 8-bar idea built from two 4-bar phrases can be one section with two inside it, and the ruler's **▸ chevron** folds between those levels. **How to write it down:** The section band's label carries the form letter; its attached note (the ✱ on the band) is where "ends open" or "answers the first phrase" goes — add the bar count too if it isn't a round 4 or 8. **Common mistakes:** Counting a pickup (a note or two before the first full bar) as bar 1, which throws off every phrase count after it. Calling two phrases a question-and-answer pair just because they're the same length — pairing is about where each one RESTS, not its size. Stopping at "there's an A and a B" without writing how many bars each one takes.

### HARMONY

**Key, numerals, cadences, bass, tension**
**What to find:** A chord's name (Gm, Cmaj7) is the surface; a **Roman numeral** (i, IV, V7) says what JOB that chord does in its key — I/i is home, V pulls toward home, IV leans away from it — and the same job sounds the same in any key, which is why numerals, not letter names, are what let you compare two songs. A **cadence** is where a phrase comes to rest, and the KIND of rest is the finding: an **authentic** cadence (V to I/i) closes all the way; a **half** cadence (ending on V) stops short, open, mid-sentence; a **plagal** cadence (IV to I) is a softer close, the "amen" motion; a **deceptive** cadence sets up V and then lands somewhere else (often vi), denying the close you expected. Underneath the chords, the **bass line** is worth reading as its own melody — a bass that walks down by step, or leaps to outline the chord, is a decision, not an accident. **Tension and release** is the harmony's push and pull across a whole phrase: which chord pulls hardest (usually V, or a chord borrowed from outside the key), and where it's allowed to let go. **How to find it in Night Roll:** Lasso the notes sounding at a moment and tap **Chord?** to see what they spell; **Challenge?** on an existing chord band shows the evidence — which label tones sound, which are missing, what else is there — so you can check a guess instead of trusting it blind. The **◯5 Circle of fifths** (View ▾ → Tools) lays out every key's chords around the wheel and shows which ones are close neighbors, useful once you know the key and want to see a chord's relatives. The key itself lives on the transport display — tap it to open the key: annotation (or "mode?" if you have the tonic but not the mode yet). **How to write it down:** A chord band's own label is the chord name; its attached note is where the Roman numeral and any "borrowed" comment goes. A cadence is a text note at the exact beat it lands — "half, stops on V" or "authentic" — or a note on the section band if the cadence is what defines the section's end. The bass-as-melody and tension/release findings are each a text note spanning the phrase they describe. **Common mistakes:** Naming the chord and stopping — a letter name with no numeral tells you the color, not the job. Calling every chord change a cadence; a cadence is specifically where a PHRASE rests, not every harmonic move along the way. Writing "tense" or "resolved" without saying which chord or beat did it. Numbering the numeral off the piece's key signature instead of the CURRENT key — a key change mid-song moves what counts as "home," so last section's IV can be this section's I.

### MELODY

**Scale degrees, shape, motifs**
**What to find:** At each phrase end (and often each downbeat), note which **scale degree** — which numbered step of the key's scale, 1 through 7 — the tune is landing on: 1 closes a phrase fully, 5 and 2 leave it open, 7 leans hard toward 1 without quite arriving. Separately, describe the melody's **shape**: is it mostly steps (one scale degree to its neighbor) or leaps, mostly rising or falling, and where does the highest note of the phrase sit — once, or repeated? A **motif** is a short recurring idea — a few notes, a rhythm, a shape — that comes back CHANGED: moved up a step, turned upside down, stretched into longer notes. Finding one means naming it and then listing every place it returns, and how each return differs from the first statement. **How to find it in Night Roll:** **find:** (View ▾ → Tools) lights up every occurrence of one pitch class across every visible track at once — built for exactly this: pick the note you think a motif turns on and watch where it recurs, with everything else dimmed so a confident zero is still an answer. Reading the notes strip while the song plays catches a shape by ear before you go hunting for it by eye. **How to write it down:** The scale-degree and shape findings are a text note spanning the phrase. A motif gets one note per return — anchor each at the bar where it starts, with what changed this time ("same shape, augmented" or "inverted, now in the bass"). **Common mistakes:** Calling every repeated idea a motif — a motif has to come back CHANGED to be worth tracking; an identical repeat is just a repeat. Describing shape in isolation from the scale degrees ("it goes up" tells you less than "it climbs from 3 to 5 to the leading tone"). Finding a motif's first appearance and never going back for the rest of its returns. Mistaking a passing decoration — a quick step off a held note and straight back — for a motif; a motif is an idea worth naming, not every ornament.

### TEXTURE & RHYTHM

**Roles, groove, the scene**
**What to find:** At any moment, which voice carries the TUNE (the melody role), which fills in the HARMONY (chords, arpeggios, repeated notes — the accompaniment role), and which holds the BASS (the lowest, usually slowest-moving voice) — and where those roles swap between tracks, which is itself worth a note. For rhythm: is there a **groove** or **ostinato** (a short pattern repeated steadily underneath); how often do the chords actually change (every bar, every beat, every two bars); and is there a bar where that pattern visibly breaks — a fill, a held note, a rest where you expected an attack? Last, ask what the SCENE under the music needs — tension, calm, forward motion, danger — and how the music supplies it; this one has no music-theory name, it's just asking what the piece is FOR. **How to find it in Night Roll:** Mute tracks one at a time (the M on each track) to isolate a voice and hear its role alone; the **Tracks view** lays every track out as a lane so you can see at a glance which one is busiest where. Nothing in the app names a role for you — this one is entirely by ear and by eye. **How to write it down:** These findings are mostly song-level rather than tied to one bar, so a text note at bar 1 (or spanning the section where roles swap) is the usual home; a role swap at a specific bar gets its own note right there instead. **Common mistakes:** Assuming the top voice is always the melody — accompaniment figures often sit high too. Noting the groove once and never checking whether it holds for the whole piece. Describing the scene for a game you haven't actually watched the music against — if you don't know the scene, say so instead of guessing. Confusing a role swap with a texture change — the same three roles can still be in play even when which track plays which one has swapped.

### SUMMARY

**What it does, and the comparison**
**What to find:** One plain paragraph, in your own words: what the piece does and why it works — not a list of the fifteen things above restated, but the one or two ideas that tie them together (a form that keeps undercutting its own cadences, say, or a bass line doing more work than the melody). Then put it beside another piece by the same composer: a shared habit — the same cadence type favored, the same kind of bass motion, the same loop plan — is usually the more durable lesson than anything true of just one piece alone. **How to find it in Night Roll:** The album list puts every piece by one composer a tap apart, so the comparison costs nothing but attention. There's no tool for the summary itself — it's the one place where you're not reading an annotation back, you're writing the conclusion the other fifteen things were building toward. **How to write it down:** A text note at bar 1, or wherever your notes-strip habit keeps song-level thoughts. **Common mistakes:** Summarizing the form again instead of saying why it works. Comparing two pieces on a surface detail (both happen to be in a minor key) instead of a compositional habit. Writing the summary before doing the other four groups — it reads thin, and it usually has to be rewritten once the harmony and melody findings are actually in.

### GETTING BETTER

**A ladder, not a syllabus**
Four rungs, each small enough to actually finish. **One group at a time:** analyze a whole piece with ONLY one group from the list above — say, every cadence and nothing else. Then the next piece, two groups. Doing all sixteen at once on piece one is how analysis stops happening. **Go back a month later:** re-read an old set of notes and add the one thing you skipped the first time — most often the Roman numeral on every chord, since that's the item that takes longest to get fluent at. **Compare two pieces, side by side:** same composer, different pieces, same list — the album view makes this one tap each way. **Ask the tutor, not for the answer:** five questions that stay inside Learning mode's rule (hints first, your own finding stands) because they ask about the CONCEPT, not your song: "what makes a cadence feel closed instead of open?" · "what's the difference between a motif and just a repeated note?" · "when does a leap in a melody feel like a question?" · "what's the difference between a period and a sentence?" · "how do I tell tension from just 'a chord I don't recognize'?" A tutor answer is a hint toward your OWN listening, not a verdict to copy into a note — the annotation still has to be the thing you heard.

### A WORKED EXAMPLE

**A made-up eight-bar loop**
Invented for this page — not a real song, not anyone's composition. Picture a made-up 8-bar loop in C major (any key would do), phrased as two 4-bar halves. **Form:** A (bars 1–4), A′ (bars 5–8) — the same phrase twice, the second time with a changed ending. Open first, closed second: that makes it a parallel period (question, then answer). **Numerals and cadences:** bars 1–4 run I – vi – IV – V, stopping on V: a half cadence, open, so the ear expects more. Bars 5–8 start the same, I – vi, then IV – V – I with the V and I sharing the last two bars: an authentic cadence, closed. The "changed ending" IS the cadence change — half the first time, authentic the second. **The bass line:** C, A, F, G under the first half; C, A, F, G, C under the second — playing the chord roots, so it reads as a simple tune of its own, not just "whatever's under the chord." **Summary:** A loop that answers itself — the first four bars ask a question by stopping on V, and the last four repeat the question but this time step from V to I and land home. The whole piece's trick is that one changed chord in the last bar does the job a whole new phrase would otherwise have to do.
